model_answer: A server adds its tools, resources and prompts as the client asks for them, over a transport the client starts. A skill adds only its name and description up front, and loads the full procedure when a task needs it. So a server is the cost you pay per tool, and a skill is cheap until it is used. I would check what the server can reach before I connect it.
prompt: A colleague wants to connect a new server and add a skill for deploy checks. Walk me through what each one puts into the context, and when.
rubric: Names what a server offers: tools, resources and prompts
Says how the client reaches the server: a transport
Says what a skill loads up front, and what waits until it is used
Says to check what a server can reach before connecting it

model_answer: I load each tool only when a step needs it, by keyword, so each call carries a few definitions. For the five round trips, I would ask whether one short program could call the tools and return one result. Before a new server connects, I read what it can reach and treat its annotations as hints, not as permissions.
prompt: Your run sends forty tool definitions with every call, and a lookup step takes five round trips. What do you change, and what do you check before you connect a new server?
rubric: Loads tools on demand instead of sending every definition
Measures the tokens and the accuracy before and after
Names programmatic calling as a way to cut round trips, without a product claim
Checks what a server can reach, and does not trust its annotations alone
